Kettle Falls, Washington Route 1. Feb. 49 Aug. 23rd 1918. Mr. O.H. Hammond Supt. Custman Ind. School Dear Sir: Your kind letter of August 13th at hand and in reply wish to say. Samuel is taking treatment from the doctor for the after effects of the serious and well-nigh fatal sicknesses of last term. We do not blame the faculty of Custman for his illness but to the damp climate of the Sound country. And Mr. Hammond asks in all sincerity if you could not recommend and have the children transferred to some other good school in the interior or in a climate more suited to Samuel's special temperament and state of health. According to his physician he needs special care and climate to avoid long trouble. Thanking you for your kindness in the past and asking your kind consideration, I beg to remain, Sincerely, Mrs. Maggie Boyd Superintendent Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Washington June 28, 1918. Mrs. Maggie Boyd Route #1 Box 49 Kettle Falls, Washington. Dear Mrs. Boyd: Your letter of the 25th., is at hand. As I wrote you day before yesterday, Sam is getting along all right and is very anxious to return home for the vacation. The other children are well at this date and appear to be enjoying themselves. We try to keep them busy enough to keep them out of mischief but not to overtax them. They have plenty of time for play as well. Don't worry about your children, Mrs. Boyd. If anything serious happens to them I will advise you promptly. Sam has been ill repeatedly but at only one time did our physician report his condition as critical. Your other children have had various spells of grippe, measles, mumps and so forth but are to all appearances enjoying themselves. They will, of course, feel downhearted at Sam's leaving them—but we will try to make them happy. Very sincerely yours Superintendent Seattle Falls, Wash. Route 1 Box 49 June 25th 1918 Dear Son, I have written before but a thick mail stream to be so irregular and ask do not hear regular from the children, and Samuel has been sick so much I am writing you again with the hope that you will get some of my letters. I wish to bring Samuel home and if you should achieve the other children also, I think from what I hear that so the climate does not agree with him and if you think It advisable I will send for the other children also. Please let me know at once and I will send tickets in either case. Now Mr. Hammond I am very anxious about Samuel as regards his health. Sophia does not think me over jealous in the matter. Waiting in suspense yours early reply I remain Truly Mrs. Maggie Boyd. Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Washington June 26, 1918. Mrs. Maggie Boyd Kettle Falls, Washington. Dear Mrs. Boyd: Samuel is again convalescing and I hope will soon be fully recovered. He was discharged from the hospital some time ago but after a few days he returned with an attack of pleurisy which later turned into pleura-pneumonia. We have him on the road to recovery however. A few weeks or a couple of months at home would help him recover more quickly. Do not worry about Samuel. We gave him the best of care and nursing and he is up and about and can travel any time you send for him. The other children are well. Very truly yours, Superintendent Kettle Falls, Wash. Route 1 Box 449 Mr. C.H. Hammond June 18-18 Dear Sir, I have a letter saying that school is out and I understand that Samuel is in the hospital. I hope that he is not very ill. I expect to bring him home for vacation. If he is in shape to come please let me know when he can come and what the fare will be to Meyers Falls. I hope the rest of the children are well. If Samuel is very ill I shall let me know at once. Truly, Mrs. Maggie Boyd Seattle Falls, Wash. Route 1 Box 449 Mrs. E. H. Hammond June 17, '18 Dear Sir, I am thinking about having Samuel come home. I would like to have all the children home for vacation but will not be able. If Samuel comes will it be necessary to deposit the return fare with you or not? It will be a convenience if I shall not need to do so. Could you inform me what the fare will be from there to Moses Falls. Also when will vacation begin. What would fare for all of them cost here. Truly, Margie Boyd Hospital Record of Samuel Boyd - June 1, 1918. February 12 - Entered with pleura-pneumonia, was dangerously ill and did not get strong enough to leave the hospital until April 7, 1918. Gained about 20 pounds. May 3 - Returned with the mumps. May 13 - Dismissed. Lost 7 pounds. May 24 - Returned with pleura pneumonia and rheumatism. While the pneumonia was in a light form, pus has formed in the right cavity which possibly may have to be drawn off. June 1 - He is running a much lower temperature than Millard and Dr. Kinnear does not consider him seriously ill. Mrs. Boyd For Dr. Kinnear Cushman Indian School, Tacoma, Washington, Feb. 15, 1918. Mrs. Maggie Boyd, Route 1, Box 49, Kettle Falls, Wash. Dear Mrs. Boyd: The children have not been sick this winter except with bad colds once or twice until just now. Juanita has German Measles, but as they last only nine days, she will be out February 20th. Sam went to the hospital with an attack of rheumatism on the 12th, but I expect he will be out in a short time. The doctor and the trained nurse will give him every possible attention, and I anticipate that by the time you receive this letter, he will be out again. You can trust me to look after your children's health, and if they become really sick, I will notify you immediately. Yours very sincerely, Superintendent Kettle Falls Wash. R. I. Box 49 Feb. 5th, 1918 Mr. E.H. Hammond. Dear Sir: I have not heard from the children for some time and when I last heard Samuel was in the hospital. So I write asking you to please let me know their condition. They seemed to be getting along fine so far as I have heard and seemed to be well satisfied. I hope that the climate there agrees with them. We have had trouble about getting letters to and from them lately but suppose that is now on the account of delay of transportation. Thanking you for past favor. I remain Respectfully Mrs. Maggie Kettle Falls, Wash. Route 1 Box 49 Mr. T.B. Wilson Dear Sir - April 14th 1917 Yours of 10 int. at hand and am sorry to hear you will close school. But will send children some time between July 1 and Sept. 10 next. I wish to know if all of the five children have been accepted so I may make preparations in time if not. In reference to Laamla whom application has sent last. Also what is necessary for me to do when I am ready to send them. With many thanks for favors. Am Truely, Mrs. Fannie Smith Boyd. Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Washington April 18, 1917. Mrs. Fannie Smith Boyd, Kettle Falls, Wash. Dear Madam: In answer to your letter of April 14, I have to say that your application for the enrollment of your five children was accepted and we can take them any time after the 1st of July, but we would prefer to have them from the 1st to the 25th of September. If you will notify me just when you want them to come, it is very probable that I can place transportation for them. I cannot say positive that I can do that until later in the season, but whenever you make your application, I will then be in a position to give you definite information as to paying their transportation. Very respectfully, Superintendent. TBW/C Hospital. Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Washington, June 1, 1918. Dear Mr. Hammond, At Dr. Kinnear's request I am sending you a report of Millard Lang's case and as Samuel Boyd's is similar tho not so serious, I have included his. Dr. Kinnear tells me that a large percentage of pneumonia cases this year are being followed by the forming of pus as in these cases. Out at the Base hospital they have many cases all of which are at once drained and which is doubtless the best procedure, but Dr. Kinnear has the parents to consider and he has reason to think that both of these cases are yielding to the treatment and the operation may not be necessary. He, however, thinks that you had better notify Millard's parents so that if drainage becomes necessary their consent may be gained. Personally, I believe that Millard is improving since yesterday morning. I think that there is no doubt but that Millard's last attack was brought on by the needless exposure. Until he became serious this time, he was a rather unruly patient but he now seems to realize that he brought his trouble on himself.
